meta.source: UESP, The Unofficial Elder Scrolls Pages (en.uesp.net), via its MediaWiki API

field_notes.word: The headword exactly as written before the first colon of the row. A row that lists several spellings ("Bahlaan, Balaan") or an optional ending ("Kel(le)") is kept as one string; word_forms only cuts it at commas and changes nothing else.
field_notes.definitions: The glosses of the row, cut at top-level commas and slashes, with reference tags removed and trailing bracketed or small-print remarks moved to notes/pos. Leading or embedded brackets are part of the gloss and stay ("(Great) Victory", "Savage(s)"). Empty when the source gives the word without a meaning. definition_text is the same text before cutting.
field_notes.pos: Only what the source states, in the source's own spelling ("v.", "verb", "adj."). Several markers on one row are joined with '; '. A marker belongs to the gloss it follows; senses[].pos says which one. The source may mean it for neighbouring glosses too.
field_notes.notes: Bracketed and small-print remarks of the row, joined with '; ' in source order. remarks[] holds them one by one with their kind (note, literal, see_also, pos), the markup they came in, their own references and the sense they follow.
field_notes.section: The letter heading (===A===) the row stands under.
field_notes.raw: The exact source line. For a phrase: its two lines joined with a newline.
field_notes.senses: One object per gloss: text, pos, separator_before (',' or '/' or null, so the source's grouping can be rebuilt), refs (the reference tags placed directly after this gloss) and refs_following (for a gloss with no tag of its own, the tags after the next gloss that has some, as in "Flow, Fly, Move{{ref}}"). Reading refs_following as covering the earlier glosses is an inference; the page does not say so.
field_notes.refs: Names of all {{ref}} tags on the row, in order; this is the field to use for 'is this row sourced at all'. An entry with no refs is unsourced on the wiki page. ref_definitions maps each name to the source it stands for (wikitext = as written, text = a plain reading of it, uses = how often the tag occurs on the whole page).
field_notes.flags: Things a reader of this file should know about the row, e.g. no_definition_in_source, template_vn (the wiki's {{vn}} marker follows the row), usage_statement_kept_as_note.
field_notes.names: name = the bold name; meaning = the text after it with ''or'' written as or; parts = the hyphen-separated English parts of the FIRST analysis; analyses[] has every analysis the source lists, with the name's own segmentation where the source gives one. Rows with no meaning are the names the page lists as untranslated (group = untranslated).
field_notes.phrases: english = the free translation without its quotation marks, or null when the source gives only a literal reading; literal = the text after 'literally:'; notes = whatever else the translation line says, in source order; translation_text = the whole line without reference tags.
field_notes.verbatim: lead_wikitext, grammar_wikitext, names_section_wikitext, notes_wikitext and references_wikitext are exact slices of the page (a section starts at its == heading line); only trailing newlines are trimmed.
field_notes.status: This file records what the wiki page says. It does not say which facts are canon: use refs and ref_definitions (game dialogue, Word Walls, official guide, developer dictionary, ...) to decide that.

translation_key_intro_wikitext: <center>Words in parentheses <small>(like in the example shown here)</small> will reference connotations or synonyms.</center>
phrases_intro_wikitext: Some phrases have a different meaning in the Dragon Language. The phrases below are examples of these phrases.
names_section_wikitext:
==Names==
Dragon names are formed of three monosyllabic words that, as a whole, may be rendered as a Shout.{{Ref|name=Esbern|[[SR:Esbern|Esbern]]'s dialogue during [[SR:Season Unending|Season Unending]] in ''[[SR:Skyrim|Skyrim]]''}} Each dragon name is unique, and so dragons are able to use these Shouts to address each other across vast distances.

While some dragon names can be definitively separated into three words, others can, interestingly enough, be translated as either three or two words. For instance, "Sahrotaar" can translate to either "Sah-Rot-Aar" (Phantom-Word-Servant/Slave) or "Sahrot-Aar" (Mighty-Servant/Slave). However, as mentioned above, dragon names are said to always be made up of three words, so one should always assume that the three-word translation is correct.

Dragon names can be translated into phrases, such as the name ''Odahviing'' (literally: Snow-Hunter-Wing), which was converted into a coherent phrase; "''Winged Snow-Hunter''".{{Ref|name=Esbern}} If other names were translated in the same way, it can be extrapolated that ''Boziikkodstrun''  would be "''Bold Storm-Wielder''" or that ''Sahloknir'' would be "''Phantom Sky-Hunter''". 

There is also the case where a mortal can be granted a ''Dovahzin'' (Dragon Name), by a dragon who believes they have earned it and it is considered a great honor. Two examples of these are [[Lore:The Vestige|Ahkahtuz]] (Hunter-Pride-Blade) and [[Lore:Ja'darri|Toshrakhat]].{{ref|name=ESONahfahlaar}} Dragon Priests also usually have names in the dragon language, although often only two syllables long instead of three.

Note that these names are not necessarily real Dragon language names. In the same way that Nahfahlaar had imperialized his name as Nafaalilargus when he worked for the Empire, it is likely that dragons who act in the employ of humans (such as Papré for the battlemage Samar Starlover, or Skakmat for the mystic [[Lore:Nulfaga|Nulfaga]]) prefer not to use dragon names during their employment. Debudjen is mentioned only in [[Lore:King_Edward|a work considered historical fiction]], and Numinex in legends [[Lore:Olaf and the Dragon|considered distorted and inconsistent]].
